message.content:
Below is a quick‑start guide you can copy/paste into your terminal (or adapt it to whatever HTTP client you prefer).  
It shows **exactly** what you asked for:

* Domain*: `test4.org`  
* Continuation cursor*: `cur456`  
* API key*: `key123`  
* Fields requested*: *only* the comment ID (`id`) and its associated “context” metadata (`context_attributes`).  

---

### 1️⃣ Build the Request URL

```text
https://api.example.com/v2/community/comments?
    domain=test4.org&
    cursor=cur456&
    fields=id,context_attributes&
    api_key=key123
```

> **Why this works**
>
> * `domain=` tells the server which site’s comments you want.  
> * `cursor=` supplies the token returned from the previous page so the next batch continues where the last one left off.  
> * `fields=` limits the payload – the service will strip out everything else, saving bandwidth & parsing time.  
> * `api_key=` authenticates you against the API gateway.

If your provider uses a different base URL or version number, just swap `https://api.example.com/v2/…` accordingly.

---

### 2️⃣ Example Using cURL

```bash
curl -sG \
     --data-urlencode "domain=test4.org" \
     --data-urlencode "cursor=cur456" \
     --data-urlencode "fields=id,context_attributes" \
     --header "Authorization: Bearer key123" \
     https://api.example.com/v2/community/comments
```

#### What each part does

| Part | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `-sG` | Silent mode + treat arguments as GET query strings |
| `--data-urlencode …` | Adds properly encoded query parameters |
| `--header "Authorization: Bearer key123"` | Passes your API key in the standard Authorization header (change to `X-Api-Key:` if required) |

---

### 3️⃣ Example Using Python requests

```python
import requests

BASE_URL   = "https://api.example.com/v2/community/comments"
PARAMS     = {
    "domain":            "test4.org",
    "cursor":            "cur456",
    "fields":            "id,context_attributes",
}
HEADERS    = {"Authorization": "Bearer key123"}   # adjust header name if needed

resp       = requests.get(BASE_URL, params=PARAMS, headers=HEADERS)
resp.raise_for_status()          # throws if status != 200

data = resp.json()
print(data["items"])             # list of comment objects
for item in data["items"]:
    print(f"id={item['id']}, ctx={item['context_attributes']}")
```

---

### 4️⃣ Typical Response Structure

Assuming the API follows common REST conventions, you’ll receive something like:

```json
{
  "next_cursor": "cur789",
  "total_count": 125,
  "items": [
      { "id": "com_00123", "context_attributes": {...} },
      { "id": "com_00456", "context_attributes": {...} }
  ]
}
```

* `next_cursor`: use this value for subsequent calls until it becomes null/empty.  
* `total_count`: optional meta‑information about total results available.  
* Each object inside `items` contains exactly the two keys you requested.

---

### 5️⃣ Things To Double‑Check

| Check | Why |
|-------|-----|
| **Endpoint path** | Some providers expose `/community/comment/list`, others `/v2/comments`. Verify in docs. |
| **Auth method** | If they expect `x-api-key: key123` instead of bearer token, change the header. |
| **Field names** | Confirm whether the field is called `context_attributes` or simply `context`. Adjust the comma‑separated list accordingly. |
| **Rate limiting** | Keep an eye on `Retry-After` headers if you hit quota limits. |

That’s all! Run either snippet, tweak the URLs/authentication per your vendor’s spec, and you’ll pull back only the IDs and their context attributes—no extra noise. Happy coding!
